label: Bathroom
rationale: The washroom routine people mention morning and night: the toilet, a shower, a bath, teeth, a shave.
mixUps: shawaa o abiru and ofuro ni hairu are both 'take a ___' in English, but a shower is poured over you (o abiru) and a bath is gone into (ni hairu); drill them in one frame, saki ni ___ kuru ne. Teeth are polished (migaku), and a shave names what comes off (hige o soru).

targets.trap: Not ofuro or basuruumu for 'bathroom': those mean the room you bathe in, which in most Japanese homes is separate from the toilet, so 'go to the bathroom' is toire ni iku.
targets.use: The plain way to excuse yourself, usually with -te kuru since you'll be back: chotto toire itte kuru. Casual speech drops ni. toire itteru means someone has gone and is in there now (tanaka-san nara toire itteru yo), not that they're on the way. With strangers or at work, otearai ni itte kimasu sounds softer.
targets.notes: Asking where it is: toire doko? to friends, otearai wa doko desu ka? to staff.

example.ja: ちょっとトイレ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm just going to the bathroom.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっとトイレに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go to the restroom.

targets.verbSense: pour over yourself, bathe in (water, sunlight)
targets.trap: Not shawaa o toru: 'take' points to toru, but a shower is poured over you, so the verb is abiru.
targets.use: Used for showering at any time of day. You mostly hear shawaa abite kuru (I'll go shower) or shawaa abita (I've showered), usually without o.
targets.notes: Casual shawaa suru is also heard.

example.romaji: saki ni shawaa abite kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にシャワー浴びてくるね。

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni shawaa o abite kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にシャワーを浴びてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and take a shower first.

targets.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
targets.trap: Not ofuro o toru or ofuro o abiru: a bath is something you go into, so it's ni hairu.
targets.use: The everyday way to talk about bathing at home, usually at night. You hear ofuro haitte kuru and ofuro haitta? (have you had your bath?) all the time, mostly without ni.
targets.notes: Running the bath is ofuro o ireru or ofuro o wakasu; the water heater announces ofuro ga wakimashita.

example.romaji: saki ni ofuro haitte kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にお風呂入ってくるね。
example.english: I'll go have my bath first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni ofuro ni haitte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にお風呂に入ってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and have my bath first.

targets.verbSense: polish, scrub until it shines (teeth, shoes)
targets.trap: Not ha o arau ('wash'): teeth are polished, migaku. hamigaki suru is just as common.
targets.use: Part of the morning and bedtime routine: ha migaita? (did you brush your teeth?), ha migaite neru (brush and go to bed). The noun form hamigaki suru is just as common.
targets.notes: 10-list-nouns leaves out bare ha (too many homophones) and names ha o migaku as the collocation card that carries it. hamigaki (brushing) and haburashi (toothbrush) are the related nouns.

example.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

examplePolite.ja: まだ歯を磨いていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

targets.trap: Not hige o kiru, which sounds like trimming it with scissors; shaving it off is soru. soru takes the hair (hige, ke, mayu) or the place (atama o soru).
targets.use: The daily shave, mostly heard as hige sotta? or hige soranakya; o is often dropped. Stubble is hige ga nobiteru (your beard's grown).
targets.notes: Growing one is hige o hayasu; hige hayashiteru = he has a beard.

example.ja: 今日ひげ剃るの忘れた。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hige o soru no o wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はひげを剃るのを忘れました。
